transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO - Nebula), Priya Desai (Lead ML Eng), Tom Becker (Infra)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix / KV cache recommendations and a cost model for Nebula Finance's conversational payments agent. Agreed to run a 24h pilot benchmark comparing no-cache vs prefix KV cache + batching on a dedicated pool. Action items and pricing to be sent.

Topics:
- High level Optimize features: continuous batching, prefix/KV cache, autoscaling, quantization suggestions
- Cost model assumptions and example numbers (tokens/sec, cost per M tokens, percent saving with KV cache)
- Deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) and security (SOC2, KMS, SSO)
- Pilot design: benchmark profile, metrics, success criteria

Action items (recapped in call): see metadata list above

Transcript:
[00:00] Sam Patel (Redwood): all right hello everyone thanks for joining, uh from Redwood, Sam here, and with me is Maya our solutions eng. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Liam O'Connor (Nebula): good thanks Sam, excited to see the optimize walkthrough — we're trying to understand how batching + the cache will impact our token costs, and what tradeoffs on latency look like
[00:24] Maya Chen (Redwood SE): great, quick agenda: i'll show how continuous batching works, then prefix / KV cache patterns, and finish with a simple cost model and pilot proposal. feel free to interrupt.
[00:36] Priya Desai (Nebula): sounds good, we're specifically worried about tail latency for interactive flows and cost for our high-volume reconciliation jobs, both matter
[00:48] Tom Becker (Nebula): and infra-wise we need VPC connectivity plus KMS integration for key management, also SSO/SAML with our okta instance
[01:02] Maya Chen: totally, we support VPC peering and a private control plane for the private deploys; for hosted/dedicated we integrate with customer KMS and provide audit logs, SOC2 fine-grained logs. i'll show where those live in the console.

[01:30] Sam Patel: quick qualification, what's your current stack for LLM inference? are you using AWS endpoints, or in-house serving?
[01:36] Liam: currently a mix — small critical flows on an OpenAI hosted api, and some experiments on self-hosted gpus, but the cost is spiking and we want predictable unit economics which is why we're looking at Redwood dedicated
[01:52] Maya: makes sense. two key levers we'll talk through: batching (which improves GPU utilization and lowers per-token cost) and prefix/KV caching (which avoids repeated autoregressive decoding for repeated prefixes in flows). combined they can be multiplicative savings depending on your workload.
[02:10] [00:02:10] Speaker 1 (transcription glitch): uh the cache is — kayv, kv, kay-v?

[02:18] Maya: yeah the acronym is KV as in key-value, sometimes transcribed as K V. for conversation agents we often cache the prefix - like the system prompt + user history - and then only decode the suffix which is usually much shorter
[02:32] Priya: our average prompt length is ~1.2k tokens but the user utterance is usually 20-60 tokens, so we were hoping cache would help
[02:44] Maya: that distribution is ideal. example numbers: on a 3k context model, if you can cache the first 1k tokens of the prefix and only decode 100 tokens most of the time, you can drop per-request token compute by ~60-75% depending on cache hit rate and batch sizes
[03:04] Tom: do you have concrete cost numbers we can plug into our finance model?
[03:10] Sam: yep i'll walk through a sample cost model. please note these are illustrative; we'll run a pilot with your traces for real numbers.

[03:20] Sam: baseline: hosted single-model no-cache, with average 100 req/s, avg output 60 tokens, total tokens including prefix 1160 per request -> that's 6,960,000 tokens per minute? sorry that's me mixing units, let me re-state. if you have 100 requests per second * 60 seconds it's 6,000 requests/minute, times 1,160 tokens ~ 6.96M tokens per minute — which is unrealistic for 100 rps, my bad, let's use per-hour numbers instead.

[03:55] Maya: (laughs) yeah we sometimes do mental math live, ok here's a cleaner frame: assume 1,000 req/hour, prefix 1,000 tokens, output 60 tokens. no cache = 1,060k tokens/hour; with prefix KV cache and 80% hit rate you only decode 60 tokens for 800 requests and full 1,060 tokens for 200 requests -> total tokens = (800*60)+(200*1060)=48k + 212k = 260k tokens/hour vs 1,060k no cache -> ~75% token reduction
[04:30] Priya: that's huge. what's the latency impact when you hit the cache vs miss?
[04:36] Maya: cache hit path avoids the prefix autoregressive decoding and can reduce GPU time dramatically. in our internal benchmarks a warm KV cache + batching improved median latency by ~30-60ms on models with long prefixes, but tail latency depends on batching policy and your allowed queuing window. with continuous batching you get small batching windows (10-30ms) that still keep p99 reasonable. if you need strict single-digit ms p99, dedicated tiny batch sizes or cpu-based endpoints might be required.
[05:10] Liam: so there's a tradeoff between batching window and p99 latency, how do you tune that?
[05:15] Maya: in the console we expose batching configs: max batch size, max wait (ms), priority routing; you can also set SLOs per route and we will route to a lower-latency pool if you override. for example, set max_wait=20ms and max_batch=32 gives you good throughput but keeps median latency low. we can share recommended presets for conversational agents.
[05:40] [05:40] Speaker 2 (Maya, botched label): and the kv cache itself supports TTL and size limits, and you can namespace per-customer to avoid cross-tenant leaks. there are also cache warmers we can run during deployments to avoid cold-start misses

[05:58] Tom: for compliance we need KMS-backed encryption of cache keys and optional in-region storage, is that supported?
[06:06] Maya: yes you can supply your KMS and we support HSM-backed keys for private deployments; cache keys and KV store encryption can be configured to use customer keys. audit logs show cache reads/writes in the console for SOC2/ISO audits.
[06:22] Priya: what about quantization and kernel choices? if we quantize to int8 does that change the cache behavior?
[06:28] Maya: cache semantics are model-agnostic; the runtime handles kernel selection and the KV cache stores activations or compressed KV shards depending on quantization. quantization impacts per-token latency but caching still yields the same relative savings because you avoid recomputing the prefix across requests.
[06:44] Liam: ok, show us the console demo and the cost model spreadsheet
[06:48] Maya: share screen?

[07:00] [07:00] Maya (screen share): opening the Optimize tab -> batching recommendations. on the left we have workload analyzer where you can upload traces or connect to a sample stream; it shows sequence length histogram and suggests batch sizes and cache hit targets. here you can see a simulated cost curve: x-axis = cache hit rate, y-axis = cost per 1M tokens. we normally illustrate that at 70% hit rate you get ~60% reduction vs no-cache depending on model and batch size

[07:36] Priya: can you export the raw numbers?
[07:40] Maya: yes export CSV, that's the spreadsheet i'll share. for the pilot we'll use your real traces and produce an apples-to-apples table: tokens decoded, GPU-seconds, latency med/p99, and estimated $/M tokens.

[07:52] Sam: quick commercial note: hosted API has per-token pricing and is easiest to get started; dedicated gives you fixed capacity and better unit economics at scale. for predictable high throughput we recommend dedicated reserved capacity plus burst. pricing details i'll send in the follow-up email.
[08:10] Liam: what's the delta on price per M tokens when moving to dedicated with typical batching and 70% cache hit? ballpark
[08:18] Sam: ballpark depends on model size; a rough example on a mid-tier open model: hosted no-cache might be $X per 1M tokens, dedicated with batching & 70% cache could be 60-70% cheaper in compute cost, after amortizing reserved capacity it often results in 40-60% lower TCO for steady workloads. we'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet for your profile.
[08:42] Priya: curious about fallback in case of cache misses and capacity constraints - does Redwood automatically route to a fallback model or region?
[08:50] Maya: yes you can define policies: fallback to a smaller quantized model, or to a hosted pool, or to a region with spare capacity. we also support canary and A/B rollouts for new model versions to ensure quality.
[09:05] Tom: we need an audit and security pack for our procurement team — SOC2 cert, penetration test summary, data residency controls
[09:12] Sam: i'll include the security pack in the follow-up and cc our security lead. we also have an enterprise SLA for dedicated customers.

[09:28] Priya: ok pilot design: recommend a 24-48h run with real traffic shaped to our peak minutes, capture p50/p95/p99, token breakdown, cache hit rate, and cost per hour. is that straightforward?
[09:38] Maya: straightforward. we can either run the pilot on Redwood hosted with a dedicated pool for you, or we can deploy private with a control-plane hook. since you need KMS and VPC, starting with Redwood Dedicated in your cloud region with VPC peering is fastest.
[09:56] Liam: timeline — we're looking to decide by end of July and ideally run the pilot next week if possible
[10:02] Sam: sounds doable. i'll send availability for pilot setup and Maya will send the benchmark template and instructions.

[10:12] [10:12] Speaker 3 (auto-caption): hmm can you share the sample numbers again, the 75% reduction, that seemed optimistic

[10:18] Maya: sure the 75% number was for the scenario of very long prefix where you cache ~1k tokens and the decoded suffix is small; realistic corporate flows often see 50-70% reductions. it scales with hit rate: 50% hit -> ~40% tokens saved; 80% hit -> ~70% saved in many of our finance customers
[10:42] Priya: any gotchas for conversational retrieval-augmented-flows? we use vector DB lookups which change the prefix sometimes
[10:50] Maya: retrieval can be cached too if the retrieval keys are stable. for dynamic retrievals with frequently changing context, you might see lower hit rates. a common pattern is hybrid: cache the static system prompt + last N messages, and separately cache frequent retrieval results. Optimize can surface which prefixes are hottest.
[11:06] Liam: competitor question: we tried a managed endpoint from AWS Sage Maker that promised batching; we saw limited savings due to cold starts. how is Redwood different?
[11:16] Maya: two parts: continuous batching (we keep persistent worker processes and avoid cold-starts) and smart kernel scheduling for long sequences. plus caching at the prefix level reduces per-request compute. also our autoscaling is GPU-aware so we avoid thundering herd cold starts.
[11:35] Tom: procurement will ask about data deletion and retention — if we evict cache keys are they wiped? and what about logs?
[11:42] Sam: yes cache evictions remove keys; we also support configurable retention windows and you can configure logs to drop payloads or mask them. audit logs are immutable but you can control retention for compliance.
[11:56] Priya: ok next steps recap?
[12:00] Sam: recap - Sam send pricing + security pack; Maya send benchmark CSV + caching guide; Priya provide sample traces and distribution; schedule pilot week of 6/28.
[12:14] Liam: looks good, thanks for the walkthrough
[12:16] Maya: thanks everyone, will follow up with the links and the spreadsheet

[12:20] End of meeting

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels, some numbers approximated in discussion; final cost estimates to be computed after pilot export.
